title: If…: the -ki- slot, and illness with its own pattern
goal: Say "if" and "while" with a single slot, name parts of the body, and tell a doctor what hurts.
bekal: saying what hurts: *kichwa kinaniuma* — the head hurts me

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hospitalini
dialogs.intro: Morning. Budi looks pale, and Amina can tell right away that something is wrong.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Habari yako? Uso wako hauonekani vizuri.
lines.id: What's the matter? You don't look well.
lines.literal: news of-you? face of-you it-not-look good.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I don't feel well. My head hurts a lot.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kidogo. Na tumbo pia linaniuma tangu jana usiku.
lines.id: A little. And my stomach has been hurting since last night, too.
lines.literal: little. and stomach also it-is-me-hurting since yesterday night.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nilikula samaki barabarani... labda hakuwa safi.
lines.id: I ate fish at a roadside stall... maybe it wasn't fresh.
lines.literal: I-past-eat fish at-road... maybe it-not-past-be clean.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Pole sana. Ukienda hospitali sasa, utapata dawa haraka.
lines.id: Poor you. If you go to the hospital now, you'll get medicine quickly.
lines.literal: patience very. you-if-go hospital now, you-will-get medicine quickly.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nikienda peke yangu, sitaweza kueleza vizuri.
lines.id: If I go by myself, I can't explain things well.
lines.literal: I-if-go alone of-me, I-not-will-can to-explain well.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: I'll come with you. Let's go right now!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kichwa na tumbo. Nina homa tangu jana.
lines.id: My head and stomach. I've had a fever since yesterday.
lines.literal: head and stomach. I-have fever since yesterday.

lines.speaker: Daktari:
lines.text: Usipokunywa maji mengi, hutapona haraka. Kunywa dawa hii mara tatu kwa siku.
lines.id: If you don't drink lots of water, you won't get better quickly. Take this medicine three times a day.
lines.literal: you-if-not-drink water much, you-not-will-recover quickly. drink medicine this times three per day.

notes: **Sijisikii vizuri is the sentence for "I don't feel well".** The infix *-ji-* means "oneself" — the same piece that makes *kujifunza* mean "to teach oneself", i.e. to learn. The positive: *ninajisikia vizuri* (I feel well).
**Tangu means "since".** *Tangu jana* (since yesterday), *tangu asubuhi* (since morning), *tangu lini?* (since when?). A question doctors always ask, so memorize your answer too.
**Peke yangu means "by myself".** Its form follows the owner: *peke yangu*, *peke yako*, *peke yake*, *peke yetu*. *Anaishi peke yake* = he/she lives alone.

**Nawe is na + wewe fused together.** Likewise *nami* (with me), *naye* (with him/her), *nasi* (with us), *nanyi* (with you pl.), *nao* (with them). A short form you'll hear a lot: *Njoo nami* (come with me).
**Mara tatu kwa siku means three times a day.** *Kwa* here means "per": *mara mbili kwa wiki* (twice a week), *shilingi elfu kwa kilo* (a thousand shillings per kilo).

grammars.title: The -ki- slot: if, and while
body: The **-ki-** slot covers two meanings: "if" for conditions, and "while" for two actions happening at once. It sits where the tense slot normally goes, and **the next clause carries the time**.

head: Sentence
Meaning
Note
rows: If you go to the market, buy bananas.
If I get money, I'll travel.
I study while listening to music.
If you don't take the medicine, you won't get better.
If I don't come, don't wait for me.

after: The negative uses the **-sipo-** slot, and the subject prefix stays the ordinary one — not a negative prefix. *Ni-sipo-fika*, *u-sipo-kunywa*, *a-sipo-kuja*, *tu-sipo-soma*. It's the only negative in Swahili that doesn't use *si-*, *hu-*, *ha-*.
*Mungu akipenda* — God willing, which you used in unit 13 — you can now read for yourself: *a-ki-penda*, "if He likes".
For a firmer or unreal condition, use **kama** (if) with an ordinary sentence: *Kama una muda, njoo* (if you have time, come). *Kama* also means "like": *kama nyumbani* (like home).

grammars.title: Pain: the body part that hurts you
body: Swahili flips the order we use. Not "I have a headache", but **"the head is hurting me"** — the body part becomes the subject, and you become the object through the *-ni-* infix from unit 15.
after: Notice that the subject prefix follows the body part's class: *kichwa* in the *ki-* class → *kinauma*; *tumbo* and *jino* in the *ji-/ma-* class → *linauma*; *miguu* and *mikono* in the *m-/mi-* class → *inauma*. Everything you set up in units 6, 9, and 16 is used again here.
The second form — *ninaumwa na…* — is easier and just as correct: *ninaumwa na kichwa*, *ninaumwa na tumbo*. If you're unsure of the class prefix, use this form.
For other complaints use *kuwa na* as in unit 14: *nina homa* (fever), *nina kikohozi* (cough), *nina mafua* (a cold), *nina kizunguzungu* (dizzy), *nina kuhara* (diarrhea), *nina mzio* (allergy).

blocks.text: Paired body parts almost all fall into the *ji-/ma-* class (*jicho → macho*, *sikio → masikio*, *jino → meno*) or the *m-/mi-* class (*mkono → mikono*, *mguu → miguu*). That's no accident: the *m-/mi-* class holds long things, and the *ji-/ma-* class holds things that come in pairs.

*Moyo* means heart in the emotional sense and in the organ sense at once — just as English "heart" does. The expressions are similar too: *moyo mkunjufu* (an open heart), *kwa moyo wote* (with all my heart), *moyo unauma* (the heart aches).

sections.title: Hospitalini na duka la dawa — at the hospital and the pharmacy

head: Kiswahili
English
rows: I've had a fever since yesterday.
I have a cold and a cough.
I've been bitten by a mosquito.
I need to be tested for malaria.
How many times should I take this medicine?

blocks.text: **Malaria is still a real risk in parts of East Africa**, and its first symptoms feel just like a bad flu: fever, chills, headache. *Ninahitaji kupima malaria* isn't an overreaction — at any clinic the test is quick and cheap, and asking for it yourself is perfectly normal.

Medicine is sold at a *duka la dawa* (pharmacy) or *famasi*. Words to recognize on labels: *kidonge* (tablet), *sharubati* (syrup), *sindano* (injection), *mara tatu kwa siku* (three times a day), *baada ya chakula* (after meals), *kabla ya kulala* (before bed).
